extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and readers of literary criticism; writers studying archetypal and formalist criticism
extracted.subtask_description: Apply Northrop Frye's taxonomy to classify and evaluate fiction by its mode (hero's power), mythos (seasonal plot types), symbolic phase, archetypal imagery, and genre, and judge works by their engagement with archetypal patterns and coherence of mode.

rubrics_metrics.name: Five Modes of Fiction (hero's power of action)
rubrics_metrics.description: Five modes defined by the hero's power of action: Mythic — Hero is a god, superior in kind to other men and the environment; Romantic — Hero is superior in degree to other men and the environment (legends, fairy tales); High Mimetic — Hero superior in degree to other men but not the environment (epic, tragedy: kings, princes); Low Mimetic — Hero is one of us (most realist novels, comedy); Ironic — Hero is inferior in power or intelligence to ourselves; we look down on them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the protagonist's relation to other men and to the environment to assign a mode; this classification is a primary dimension for reading tone and convention. (Frye notes Western literature has shifted progressively from mythic to ironic.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Four Mythoi (plots tied to seasons)
rubrics_metrics.description: Four plot-myths mapped to seasons: Comedy / Spring — myth of birth, renewal, integration; ends in marriage/feast; Romance / Summer — myth of triumph, adventure, quest, harmony; Tragedy / Autumn — myth of fall, decay, isolation, sacrifice; Irony and Satire / Winter — myth of chaos, dissolution, the absurd.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify a work's dominant plot-pattern by its corresponding mythos/season. Frye emphasizes these mythoi form a circular pattern matching the seasonal cycle, useful for understanding plot movement and thematic orientation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theory of Symbols (Five Phases)
rubrics_metrics.description: Five phases of symbolic meaning: Literal / Descriptive — symbol as motif (within the work) or sign (pointing outward); Formal — symbol as image; structural play of imagery; Mythical / Archetypal — symbol as connector across literary tradition; Anagogic — symbol as monad; literature as a unified imaginative universe; (Ethical phase implicit between formal and mythical).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate symbols by their phase: are they local motifs, part of a work's internal imagery, linked to broader archetypes, or pointing to transcendent/unifying meanings? Note Frye's acknowledgement of an implicit ethical phase between formal and mythical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Archetypal Imagery (apocalyptic, demonic, analogical; Great Chain of Being)
rubrics_metrics.description: Archetypal imagery categories include Apocalyptic imagery (paradise, the Lamb, the Tree of Life, bread/wine, the city, the garden), Demonic imagery (hell, the predator, the wasteland, sterile city, dragon), and Analogical imagery (states resembling but not identical to either pole). Organized by the Great Chain of Being: divine, human, animal, vegetable, mineral, water.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess how richly a work employs archetypal images and where its images locate on the Great Chain of Being; examine whether imagery leans toward apocalyptic, demonic, or an intermediate/analogical state to determine symbolic valence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theory of Genres (Four Radicals of Presentation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Four radicals of presentation defining genres: Epos — author addresses visible audience directly (oral, recited); Fiction — author and audience hidden from each other (the novel); Drama — author hidden; audience experiences action directly; Lyric — speaker overheard by hidden audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify a work by its mode of address/presentation. Frye links each genre to a distinctive rhythm: recurrence (epos), continuity (fiction/prose), decorum (drama), associative (lyric). Use these rhythms to evaluate formal expectations and effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluative use: classification and judgment by archetypal engagement and mode coherence
rubrics_metrics.description: A work can be classified by mode, mythos, symbolic phase, and genre — and judged by how richly it engages archetypal patterns and how coherently it inhabits its mode.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating a work, map it across Frye's dimensions (mode, mythos, symbolic phase, genre) and then judge: (1) richness of engagement with archetypal patterns (variety, depth, resonance of archetypal images/symbols), and (2) coherence in inhabiting its assigned mode/genre (consistency of conventions, tonal unity). Use mismatches (e.g., incoherent mode, shallow archetypal use) as grounds for critique.
